html:
The First Hijra, or migration to Abyssinia, was the flight of a group of early Muslims from Mecca to the Christian kingdom of Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, around 613 to 615. Its Christian king gave them refuge.

In Mecca the followers of the prophet Muhammad faced growing persecution from the Quraysh, the tribe that ruled the city. Muhammad, so Islamic tradition says, advised some of them to go to Abyssinia, whose king was just and would wrong no one. A first party of about eleven men and four women crossed the Red Sea; a larger group followed later.

Islamic sources tell how the Quraysh sent envoys with gifts to ask the king, called the Najashi (the Negus), to hand the refugees back. He heard both sides. Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, a cousin of Muhammad, spoke for the Muslims and recited a passage of the Qur'an about Mary, the mother of Jesus. The king was moved and refused to give them up. Modern historians have tried to match the Najashi with Aksumite kings known from coins, such as Armah, without certainty.

Some of the exiles came back to Mecca and joined Muhammad's later Hijra to Medina in 622. Others stayed in Aksum until 628.

The episode shows how closely Arabia and the Horn of Africa were linked across the Red Sea, by trade and by Aksum's earlier rule in Yemen. Muslim tradition remembers the Christian king with respect, and the town of Negash in Tigray, where he is said to be buried, holds one of the oldest mosques in Africa.
